We light no fire to warm the past,
no lamp to make its shadows kind;
we stand where silence held its breath
and ask our hearts to look, and mind.

Names—more than numbers—thread the air,
a murmured roll the years can’t still:
each syllable a broken world,
each absence a remaining will.

Here, hatred learned to speak in laws,
in paperwork and polished lies,
in uniforms and neighbor’s doors,
in trains that did not ask “who cries?”

Intolerance, a patient seed,
was watered daily, made to bloom
in casual jokes, in measured scorn,
until it flowered into doom.

And how it spread: not sudden flame,
but ash that drifted street to street—
the shrinking circle of “us” and “them,”
the practiced turning of one’s feet.

Remembering is not a shrine
that locks the grief behind a glass;
it is a vow with open eyes:
no world is safe because it “passed.”

nor to be clean in borrowed tears;
we look because forgetting feeds
the oldest hunger of our fears.

and let the witness be our guide:
when any life is marked as less,
the doorway to the dark stands wide.

Stand, when a neighbor is denied.
Teach, when a child is told to hate.
Refuse the lie that some must hide.

For what was done was done by hands
that resembled ours in work and prayer—
and what can rise again begins
where we decide we do not care.

We carry not only mourning now,
but warning, stitched into our days:
that love is ordinary labor,
and justice is a thousand ways.

Let memory be more than grief—
let it be courage, clear and stern:
to name the dead, protect the living,
and make of “Never” something learned.

We light no fire to warm the past,
no lamp to make its shadows kind;
we stand where silence held its breath
and ask our hearts to look, and mind.

Names—more than numbers—thread the air,
a murmured roll the years can’t still:
each syllable a broken world,
each absence a remaining will.

Here, hatred learned to speak in laws,
in paperwork and polished lies,
in uniforms and neighbor’s doors,
in trains that did not ask “who cries?”

Intolerance, a patient seed,
was watered daily, made to bloom
in casual jokes, in measured scorn,
until it flowered into doom.

And how it spread: not sudden flame,
but ash that drifted street to street—
the shrinking circle of “us” and “them,”
the practiced turning of one’s feet.

Remembering is not a shrine
that locks the grief behind a glass;
it is a vow with open eyes:
no world is safe because it “passed.”

We do not look to borrow pain,
nor to be clean in borrowed tears;
we look because forgetting feeds
the oldest hunger of our fears.

So let the record be our mirror,
and let the witness be our guide:
when any life is marked as less,
the doorway to the dark stands wide.

Speak, when the slur is called “a joke.”
Stand, when a neighbor is denied.
Teach, when a child is told to hate.
Refuse the lie that some must hide.

For what was done was done by hands
that resembled ours in work and prayer—
and what can rise again begins
where we decide we do not care.

We carry not only mourning now,
but warning, stitched into our days:
that love is ordinary labor,
and justice is a thousand ways.

Let memory be more than grief—
let it be courage, clear and stern:
to name the dead, protect the living,
and make of “Never” something learned.
